title: Broken: a slow lakehouse table made of many small files
objective_text: Find why a Delta table is slow to read, compact its small files without losing or doubling rows, and keep its history.
scenario: Device events arrive in 40 small batches a day, and the ingestion job appends each one as it lands. Readers complain the table gets slower every day. The table has the right rows; it's how they're stored that hurts.
engine_label: Python with delta-rs and Polars on this PC
verifies: Your script ran on this PC and left a Delta table with at most 2 data files, an OPTIMIZE in its history after the writes, and all 1,000 events once each.
does_not_verify: Read speed in Fabric: this checks file counts in the Delta log, not query timings. V-Order and the lakehouse's table maintenance (OPTIMIZE and VACUUM) in Fabric are separate features.
Statistics and their effect on the SQL analytics endpoint.

fault.summary: Each batch is a separate append, so the table holds 40 tiny data files and every read opens all of them.
fault.symptom: tables/events has 40 data files for 1,000 rows.

Events were lost or doubled while repairing the table.

hints: How many data files does the table have? DeltaTable(TABLE).file_uris() lists them.
Rewriting the data yourself risks losing or doubling rows. Delta has a maintenance operation for exactly this.
DeltaTable(TABLE).optimize.compact() rewrites small files into large ones as one OPTIMIZE commit; the rows don't change.
explanation: Every append adds at least one data file, and every reader opens every file, so a table fed by many small writes slows down even when the rows are right. Compaction (OPTIMIZE) rewrites many small files into a few large ones in one commit, without changing the rows, and the old files stay in the history until they are vacuumed. In Fabric, OPTIMIZE in a notebook or the lakehouse's table maintenance does the same; batching writes upstream prevents the problem in the first place.
